query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing traditional EAM reference potentials with a machine‐learned interatomic potential trained on extensive ab initio data across the solid and liquid configurations of high‐entropy alloys near their melting temperatures will improve phase‐space overlap and reduce thermodynamic‐integration path mismatch.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both their solid state and ab initio liquid state near high melting temperatures
generation.intervention: Adopt a machine-learning potential (e.g., a neural network or Gaussian approximation potential) as the reference system for thermodynamic integration instead of conventional EAM potentials
generation.conditions: Applicable to HEAs with five or more principal elements at temperatures at and just above the melting point, where the liquid exhibits a wide diversity of atomic configurations
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential, by being trained on ab initio data encompassing many local environments, mediates the transformation between the reference and target phase spaces by accurately representing configurations that classical EAM models fail to capture
generation.mechanism: Since the machine-learned potential is fitted to a large, diverse training set sampled from ab initio calculations (including many rare or transient configurations in the liquid), it provides a closer match to the energy landscape of the target system. This improved representation increases overlap in phase space between the reference and target states, thereby reducing the integration path mismatch during free-energy computations.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in thermodynamic integration path mismatch (potentially on the order of an order of magnitude improvement relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references) and more reliable free-energy differences between phases, with better convergence in simulations
generation.baseline: TOR-TILD’s EAM reference approach that suffers from limited configurational representation of the ab initio liquid phase
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is expected for HEAs of complex compositions in regimes close to the melting temperatures; outside these conditions (e.g., at extreme temperatures or compositions far from the training data domain) the advantage may diminish or require further potential refinement
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in integration mismatch is uncertain and will depend on the quality and range of the ab initio data used for training, as well as the chosen ML methodology and its transferability under extreme conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Perform thermodynamic integration for a selected HEA by (a) using the standard EAM (TOR-TILD) approach and (b) using the ML potential approach. Compare the free-energy differences computed along the integration path against a direct ab initio molecular dynamics evaluation or an independent experimental free-energy benchmark.
measurements: Convergence behavior of the free-energy integration path
Computed free-energy differences between solid and liquid phases
Phase-space overlap metrics (e.g., distribution of sampled configurations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML potential does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in phase-space overlap—as evidenced by a reduction in integration path mismatch and improved convergence of free-energy differences relative to the EAM approach—the hypothesis will be falsified
